title: The olive tree (Romans 11)
hook: Gentiles are grafted into Israel's olive tree; God's gifts are irrevocable

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's grief for his own people, and your line was beautiful feet. Did you carry a piece of good news to someone on purpose? Day three hundred twenty-five.

Picture an olive tree on a hillside in the Holy Land. Some of them there are centuries old: trunks twisted like rope, still bearing fruit. A farmer who wants a better tree doesn't plant a new one. He cuts a branch, and fits a new one into the wound, and binds it, and waits. That's grafting. The new branch lives on the old root's water and strength. Paul, still wrestling with the question from yesterday, has one more thing to say about his people and the new Gentile believers in Rome. And he says it with a tree.
screen: `AN OLIVE TREE, CENTURIES OLD.` → `A NEW BRANCH FITTED INTO THE WOUND.` → `PAUL SAYS IT WITH A TREE.`

segments.voice: Paul opens chapter eleven with a question, in the King James Bible: "I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid." His answer is no, and he's his own proof: I'm an Israelite too, he says. Then the tree. Israel is a cultivated olive tree, rooted in the promises to Abraham. Some of its natural branches, he says, have been broken off. And Gentile believers, people from the nations, are like shoots from a wild olive, grafted in among the branches, drawing life from the root. Here's the surprising part: that's backward. Farmers usually graft a good branch onto a wild root, not a wild branch onto a good one. Paul knows it. He calls it contrary to nature. The Gentiles got in by a move no farmer would make. Then Paul turns to the newcomers in Rome, who may have been getting proud, and he warns them: "Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee." You don't hold up the tree. The tree holds you. And then a line many Christians and Jews in conversation today treasure: "For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance." Without repentance means God doesn't take them back. Paul even hopes the broken branches will be grafted in again, and he says that all Israel shall be saved, though Christians differ on what he meant by that. And then, having thought as hard as he can, Paul stops thinking and starts praising: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" When his argument reaches its edge, he doesn't pretend to have it all figured out. He bows.
screen: `HATH GOD CAST AWAY HIS PEOPLE?` · `A WILD BRANCH, GRAFTED IN.` · `CONTRARY TO NATURE.` · `THE GIFTS OF GOD ARE NOT TAKEN BACK.` · then, large: `THOU BEAREST NOT THE ROOT, BUT THE ROOT THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor your spiritual roots. Settle, and breathe. Think about where your own faith, or your questions, or your sense of right and wrong came from. A grandmother who prayed. A teacher. A congregation. A tradition much older than you, that someone carried to you across centuries. Picture those roots under you, like the old olive tree's. You didn't grow them. They're holding you. Name one of them, and give thanks. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. The bell holds the time.
The olive tree. Paul's picture of Israel, rooted in God's promises, with wild branches grafted in against nature, all drawing life from the same root.

Your line: you don't support the root. Today, when you feel a little proud of what you know or believe, remember who carried it to you, and thank one of them if you can. Day three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Many Christians speak of the Jewish roots of their faith, and some churches mark this with study of the Hebrew Scriptures, Jewish-Christian dialogue, and reflection on Romans 11 during Holocaust remembrance.

original.note: Greek: wild olive. Paul's picture of the Gentiles, grafted into the cultivated tree.

trapdoor: what you thought: the olive tree is a picture of the church replacing Israel.
what it means: Paul pictures Israel as the tree, with Gentiles grafted in and supported by its root, and says God's gifts and calling are not taken back.
what a scholar hears: some ancient farm writers mention grafting wild olive onto a failing tree to renew it, but Paul himself calls his graft contrary to nature.

notes: SENSITIVE DAY. The olive tree has been read both in supersessionist and non-supersessionist ways; the trapdoor names the 'replacement' reading only as a mistaken first impression. Keeper should decide whether this is fair to all Christian readers.
'All Israel shall be saved' (11:26) is paraphrased with 'Christians differ on what he meant'. Confirm.
Grafting: normal practice grafts cultivated scions onto wild rootstock; Columella (De Re Rustica 5.9) mentions grafting wild olive onto a failing tree. Confirm the trapdoor.
'Some of them there are centuries old': confirm; avoid naming specific ages.
'A line many Christians and Jews in conversation today treasure' (11:29): cited in Catholic documents on Judaism; confirm phrasing.
